HEAD_NECK.label: Head & neck
HEAD_NECK.description: The muscles that turn and tilt your head, hold it upright against gravity all day, and let you chew and make facial expressions.
HEAD_NECK.whyItMatters: Hours of looking down at a phone or laptop force these muscles to hold your head forward instead of stacked over your spine. Over time that's linked to chronic neck strain and tension headaches.

exercise.name: Isometric neck exercise
exercise.cue: Press your forehead gently into your own hand without letting your head move, hold a few seconds, then do the same from the back of your head. You're training the muscle to resist force, not moving the joint at all.

SHOULDER.label: Shoulders
SHOULDER.description: A small, highly mobile group of muscles capping the shoulder joint, letting you lift your arm out to the side, forward, and overhead.
SHOULDER.whyItMatters: The shoulder trades stability for range of motion, which makes it one of the most commonly injured joints. Keeping these muscles balanced and strong is one of the main things that protects it.

exercise.name: Arm circles
exercise.cue: Stand with arms out to your sides at shoulder height, and trace slow circles about the size of a dinner plate. Do ten circles forward, then ten backward.

CHEST.label: Chest
CHEST.description: The muscles across the front of your ribcage. They power pushing movements and help hold your shoulders and upper back in a neutral position.
CHEST.whyItMatters: When chest and upper-back muscles are both weak, the chest tends to win, pulling the shoulders forward into a rounded, slouched posture.

exercise.name: Incline push-up
exercise.cue: Place your hands on a sturdy elevated surface like a bench or step, walk your feet back so your body forms a straight line, then lower your chest toward the edge and push back up. The higher the surface, the easier the exercise.
exercise.equipmentNote: Needs a stable elevated surface (bench, step, sturdy table).

BACK.label: Back
BACK.description: A large group running from your shoulder blades down to your lower spine. They pull, support an upright posture, and balance out all the pushing muscles at the front of your body.
BACK.whyItMatters: This is one of the biggest muscle groups in the upper body, so training it meaningfully adds to your body's overall capacity to use blood sugar. It also directly supports the spine — weak back muscles are a common contributor to lower back pain.

exercise.name: Chin-up
exercise.cue: Hang from a bar with palms facing you, then pull your chest toward the bar by squeezing your shoulder blades down and together — think of the pull coming from your back, not just your arms.
exercise.equipmentNote: Needs a pull-up bar. If you can't do a full rep yet, hang and practice the squeezing motion first.

UPPER_ARM.label: Upper arms
UPPER_ARM.description: The biceps at the front and triceps at the back of your upper arm. They bend and straighten your elbow, and are behind almost everything you carry, lift, or push.
UPPER_ARM.whyItMatters: These muscles matter less for metabolism and more for staying functionally independent — carrying groceries, lifting yourself out of a chair, or catching your balance all rely on them staying strong as you age.

exercise.name: Bench dips
exercise.cue: Sit on the edge of a bench with hands beside your hips, slide forward, and lower your body by bending your elbows until they're close to a right angle, then press back up.
exercise.equipmentNote: Needs a sturdy bench or step.

FOREARM.label: Forearms
FOREARM.description: The muscles between your elbow and wrist that control wrist movement and, together with the hand, your grip.
FOREARM.whyItMatters: Grip strength specifically has been studied as a simple marker of overall muscular health in large population studies, where lower grip strength was associated with higher risk of health complications later in life. It's a signal worth paying attention to, not a guarantee either way.

exercise.name: Wrist circles
exercise.cue: Extend your arms out to your sides at shoulder height, palms down, and rotate just your wrists in slow circles — ten one way, then ten the other.

ABDOMEN.label: Abdomen
ABDOMEN.description: The muscles wrapping your midsection, including the ones people call "abs." They flex your spine and help brace your trunk during almost any movement.
ABDOMEN.whyItMatters: A weak core is one of the most consistently identified contributors to lower back pain, especially for people who sit for long stretches during the day.

exercise.name: 3/4 sit-up
exercise.cue: Lie on your back with knees bent and feet anchored, then curl your torso up toward your knees, stopping about three-quarters of the way instead of coming all the way forward, before lowering back down with control.

HIP.label: Hips & glutes
HIP.description: The glutes and surrounding hip muscles — among the largest and most powerful muscles in the body. They extend your hip and keep your pelvis stable every time you stand, walk, or climb stairs.
HIP.whyItMatters: Because this is some of the largest muscle mass in the entire body, training it is one of the more effective ways to increase how much blood sugar your muscles can absorb after a meal. Weak glutes are also commonly linked to knee and lower back strain, especially with a lot of daily sitting.

exercise.name: Glute bridge
exercise.cue: Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat, then push through your heels to lift your hips until your body forms a straight line from shoulders to knees, squeezing your glutes at the top before lowering slowly.

UPPER_LEG.label: Upper legs
UPPER_LEG.description: The quadriceps at the front and hamstrings at the back of your thigh. They straighten and bend your knee, and do most of the work in standing up, walking, and climbing stairs.
UPPER_LEG.whyItMatters: This is typically the single largest muscle group in the body by mass, which makes it the biggest single lever for improving how well your body manages blood sugar and responds to insulin.

exercise.name: 90/90 hamstring raise
exercise.cue: Lying on your back, bend one leg to a right angle at the hip and knee, then straighten that leg up toward the ceiling and back down, keeping the hip bent the whole time. Repeat, then switch legs.

LOWER_LEG.label: Lower legs
LOWER_LEG.description: Your calf muscles, running down the back of your lower leg. They point your foot and are what push you off the ground with every step, run, or jump.
LOWER_LEG.whyItMatters: Strong calves contribute to balance and stability, which becomes more important for fall prevention as people get older.

exercise.name: Standing calf raise
exercise.cue: Stand with the balls of your feet on a step edge (or flat ground if you're just starting), rise up onto your toes as high as you can, hold briefly, then lower back down with control. Hold a wall or chair for balance.
exercise.equipmentNote: No equipment needed — a step edge adds range of motion but isn't required.

HAND.label: Hand
HAND.description: The small muscles inside your hand that let you grip, pinch, and control individual fingers with precision.
HAND.whyItMatters: These muscles are behind fine motor tasks like opening jars, buttoning a shirt, or holding a pen — the kind of everyday independence that becomes more noticeable as grip strength declines with age.

FOOT.label: Foot
FOOT.description: The small muscles that support your arch and control your toes, working with the lower leg to keep you balanced on uneven ground.
FOOT.whyItMatters: Foot muscle strength contributes to balance and is linked to conditions like plantar fasciitis when it's neglected.

TRUNK.label: Trunk
TRUNK.description: The deep muscles between your ribs and the diaphragm underneath your lungs — the main muscles responsible for breathing and for bracing your trunk under load.
TRUNK.whyItMatters: The diaphragm is your primary breathing muscle. Training trunk stability alongside it supports both breathing efficiency and the ability to brace your spine safely during effort.

exercise.name: Plank
exercise.cue: Support your body on your forearms and toes with a straight line from shoulders to ankles, and hold the position, breathing normally, for as long as you can keep good form.
